passages.t: Restore gently, and carry one another's burdens
passages.happening:
“Brothers, if someone is caught in a trespass, you who are spiritual should restore him with a spirit of gentleness. But watch yourself, or you also may be tempted” (verse 1).

“Carry one another’s burdens, and in this way you will fulfill the law of Christ” (verse 2).

Paul warns against thinking too highly of yourself. “If anyone thinks he is something when he is nothing, he deceives himself” (verse 3). Each one should test his own work, and not compare himself with others (verse 4). “For each one should carry his own load” (verse 5).
passages.hearers:
Paul has just named the fruit of the Spirit. Now he shows what it looks like when someone in the church goes wrong.

‘Caught’ can mean caught in the act, or caught off guard, overtaken by a sin. ‘You who are spiritual’ may be gently ironic. Some in Galatia may have thought themselves more spiritual than others. Paul says that the truly spiritual show it by how they treat a person who has fallen.

‘Restore’ is the word used for setting a broken bone or mending a fishing net. The aim is to make the person whole again, not to punish or expose them. And it must be done ‘with a spirit of gentleness’, one of the fruit of the Spirit.

‘Watch yourself’ is a warning against pride. The one who corrects can fall too.

‘The law of Christ’ is a striking phrase in a letter that warns against the law. Paul means the way of life Christ taught and lived, summed up in love (5:14). Christ carried our burdens. His people carry each other's.

Verses 2 and 5 can sound as if they disagree. They do not. A ‘burden’ in verse 2 is a heavy weight, too much for one person. A ‘load’ in verse 5 is the pack each person carries, their own work and responsibility before God. Help each other with what crushes; do not hand off what is yours to carry.
passages.ot:
The law told Israel to deal honestly and kindly with a brother who goes wrong: “Directly rebuke your neighbor, so that you will not incur guilt on account of him” (Leviticus 19:17).

When Nathan confronted David, he did it so that David could repent. And when David confessed, the word came at once: “The LORD has taken away your sin,” Nathan replied (2 Samuel 12:13). Restoration was the goal.

The psalms speak of God as the one who carries his people's load: “Blessed be the Lord, who daily bears our burden” (Psalm 68:19).
passages.hard:
What does ‘restore him with a spirit of gentleness’ mean when someone has done serious harm?

Paul is speaking of a believer overtaken by sin, and of the church's aim: to bring that person back, humbly and kindly. That is a beautiful thing, and churches should practise it.

But this verse has sometimes been misused to keep serious wrongs quiet, or to put a person who has harmed others straight back where they can do harm again. That is not what Paul means. Restoring a person to Christ is not the same as restoring them to a position of trust. Gentleness toward the one who fell never means carelessness toward the ones who were hurt. Abuse and other crimes are reported to the police and the proper authorities. The site's note on 1 Corinthians 5:1-5 says more about this.

If you have been harmed by someone in a church, and were told to forgive and say nothing, what happened to you may have been wrong. Please talk with someone you trust outside that situation. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
passages.asks: Paul says the spiritual person is known by gentleness toward someone who has fallen. Ask how you respond when another believer fails: with gossip, with distance, or with gentleness. Ask whose burden you could help carry this week. And ask what load is yours to carry, which you have been trying to hand to someone else.

passages.t: Sowing and reaping, and doing good to all
passages.happening:
“Nevertheless, the one who receives instruction in the word must share in all good things with his instructor” (verse 6).

“Do not be deceived: God is not to be mocked. Whatever a man sows, he will reap in return” (verse 7). Sowing to please the flesh reaps destruction; “but the one who sows to please the Spirit, from the Spirit will reap eternal life” (verse 8).

“Let us not grow weary in well-doing, for in due time we will reap a harvest if we do not give up” (verse 9). “Therefore, as we have opportunity, let us do good to everyone, and especially to the family of faith” (verse 10).
passages.hearers:
Verse 6 is practical. Those who taught the faith gave their time, and those they taught were to share ‘all good things’ with them, food, money and help. Paul often worked to support himself, but he taught that the church should care for its teachers (1 Corinthians 9:14).

Sowing and reaping was a picture every hearer knew. A farmer who plants barley does not harvest wheat. And the harvest comes only after long patience. Paul applies it to the whole of life. What we give ourselves to, we become.

‘Sows to please the flesh’ means living for oneself. ‘Sows to please the Spirit’ means living in step with God's Spirit, in the ways chapter 5 described. One road ends in ruin. The other ends in ‘eternal life’, the life of the age to come.

‘Grow weary’ and ‘give up’ are honest words. Doing good can be tiring and seem to change nothing. Paul promises a harvest ‘in due time’, God's time.

‘The family of faith’ uses the language of a household. Believers are family. In Paul's world households were expected to provide for their own members first. Paul says: do good to everyone, and do not neglect your own brothers and sisters.
passages.ot:
Scripture often speaks of sowing and reaping. “He who sows injustice will reap disaster” (Proverbs 22:8). Hosea warned Israel, “For they sow the wind, and they shall reap the whirlwind” (Hosea 8:7). And on the bright side, “A generous soul will prosper, and he who refreshes others will himself be refreshed” (Proverbs 11:25).

Care for those who work is in the law too: “Do not muzzle an ox while it is treading out the grain” (Deuteronomy 25:4), a verse Paul uses for paying those who teach (1 Corinthians 9:9).
passages.hard:
Does ‘whatever a man sows, he will reap’ mean that giving money will make you rich?

No. Paul is speaking of a whole life sown to the flesh or to the Spirit, and the harvest he names is ‘eternal life’, not wealth. The ‘good things’ of verse 6 are shared to support teachers, not offered as a deal with God. Some teaching promises that money given to God, or to a ministry, will come back many times over. That is prosperity teaching, and it is an error. It turns grace into a transaction, and it has hurt many people who gave what they could not afford. Paul boasts only in the cross (verse 14).

Nor does the verse mean that every hardship is a harvest of a person's own sin. Job's friends said that, and God said they were wrong (Job 42:7).

If you gave money under pressure, or because you were promised a return, that was not your failure. If it still weighs on you, please talk with a pastor or friend you trust. These notes are not financial advice. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
passages.asks: Paul says that what we sow, we reap. Ask what you are sowing with your time, your attention and your money. And if you are tired of doing good, hear Paul's promise: in due time there will be a harvest. Who is the ‘everyone’ you have opportunity to do good to this week?

passages.t: In Paul's own hand: boasting only in the cross
passages.happening:
“See what large letters I am using to write to you with my own hand!” (verse 11).

Paul names what the teachers are really doing. “Those who want to make a good impression outwardly are trying to compel you to be circumcised. They only do this to avoid persecution for the cross of Christ” (verse 12). They do not keep the law themselves, he says, “yet they want you to be circumcised that they may boast in your flesh” (verse 13).

“But as for me, may I never boast, except in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ, through which the world has been crucified to me, and I to the world” (verse 14). “For neither circumcision nor uncircumcision means anything. What counts is a new creation” (verse 15).

“Peace and mercy to all who walk by this rule, even to the Israel of God” (verse 16).
passages.hearers:
Here Paul takes the pen from the scribe who wrote the letter down, and writes the ending himself, in large letters. Why large is not known. It may be his eyesight, or hands hardened by work and beatings, or simply emphasis, like writing in bold.

Verse 12 gives Paul's reading of the teachers' motives. If they could show that Gentile believers had been circumcised, they would look faithful in the eyes of those who might otherwise persecute them. Paul is not speaking of Jews in general. He is speaking of these teachers, believers in Jesus, who he thinks were avoiding the cost of the cross.

‘Boast’ in Paul's world meant to take pride in, to rest your standing on. People boasted of family, city, wealth and honours. The teachers wanted to boast in the Galatians' circumcision, a mark of success. Paul will boast in one thing: a Roman cross, the most shameful death the world knew.

‘The world has been crucified to me, and I to the world’. The cross ended Paul's old way of measuring worth. The world's ranks and marks no longer hold him, and he no longer lives for them.

‘New creation’ sums up the letter. Neither having the mark nor lacking it counts. What counts is that God, through Christ, is making all things new, starting with people.

‘This rule’ is a word for a measuring line, a standard. Paul blesses all who live by the measure of the cross and the new creation.
passages.ot:
Paul's blessing echoes the prayers of Israel. Two psalms end, “Peace be upon Israel” (Psalm 125:5; Psalm 128:6). And Isaiah heard God promise, “My loving devotion will not depart from you, and My covenant of peace will not be broken” (Isaiah 54:10).

‘New creation’ takes up Isaiah's promise: “For behold, I will create new heavens and a new earth” (Isaiah 65:17).

And boasting only in the Lord is the word of Jeremiah: “But let him who boasts boast in this, that he understands and knows Me” (Jeremiah 9:24).
passages.hard:
Who is ‘the Israel of God’ in verse 16?

The phrase is found nowhere else in the Bible, and Christians read it in more than one way. These notes set out the main readings and do not choose.

Many read it as the whole church, Jewish and Gentile believers together. Paul has called all who belong to Christ ‘Abraham's seed’ (3:29) and ‘children of promise’ (4:28). On this reading the little Greek word kai means ‘even’, as the BSB has it: those who walk by this rule are the Israel of God.

Others point out that Paul nowhere else calls the church ‘Israel’, and that kai most often means ‘and’, as many other English Bibles have it. On their reading, Paul blesses all believers and then adds a blessing on Jewish believers in Jesus in particular.

A third reading takes ‘the Israel of God’ as the Jewish people as a whole, on whom Paul prays God's mercy, as in Romans 11, where he says that “all Israel will be saved” (Romans 11:26).

The question touches how Christians understand the church and Israel, on which faithful traditions differ. The site's notes on Romans 9 to 11 set out those views. On every reading, Paul's point stands: belonging to God's people comes through Christ, not through a mark on the body. And no reading gives any ground for contempt for the Jewish people. Paul, a Jew, blesses Israel with peace and mercy.
passages.asks: Paul says he will boast in nothing but the cross. Ask what you quietly rest your worth on: your family, your work, your church, your side, your record. Then ask what it would mean for the world to be crucified to you, so that its measures no longer rule you. What would a ‘new creation’ look like in your life this year?

passages.t: The marks of Jesus, and grace
passages.happening:
“From now on let no one cause me trouble, for I bear on my body the marks of Jesus” (verse 17).

And Paul ends as he began, with grace. “The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with your spirit, brothers. Amen” (verse 18).
passages.hearers:
‘Marks’ is the Greek word stigmata. It was used for brands or tattoos put on slaves to show who owned them, and sometimes on soldiers or on worshippers of a god. Paul's marks are the scars of his sufferings for Christ. He was stoned at Lystra and left for dead (Acts 14:19), and he was beaten and whipped more than once (2 Corinthians 11:24-25). If the letter went to the churches of the south, some of the Galatians may have seen those wounds for themselves.

The teachers wanted the Galatians to bear the mark of circumcision. Paul bears a different mark, the marks of belonging to Jesus.

After all the sharp words, the last word before the ‘Amen’ is ‘brothers’. He has argued, warned and rebuked. But they are still family, and he commits them to the grace of the Lord Jesus Christ.
passages.ot:
Isaiah pictures people writing on their own hands that they belong to God: “still another will write on his hand, ‘The LORD’s,’ and will take the name of Israel” (Isaiah 44:5).

And the blessing of grace echoes the priestly blessing of Israel: “May the LORD bless you and keep you; may the LORD cause His face to shine upon you and be gracious to you” (Numbers 6:24-25).
passages.asks:
Paul's marks show whose he is. Ask what in your life shows that you belong to Jesus, not to win anyone's approval, but because following him has cost you something. And hear the last word of the letter as spoken to you: grace, from the Lord Jesus Christ, to his brothers and sisters.

The next letter in the Bible, Ephesians, takes up the same great theme in a quieter voice: Jews and Gentiles made one new people in Christ.
